top_categories.workout_context: 3000 miles. Your legs will beg to quit after 120. This trains the power output you need from mile 130 onward.
Every hard session works better with a bigger aerobic base. At 3000 miles, base fitness is the difference between racing and surviving.
175,000ft of climbing makes aerobic ceiling relevant when the grade or pace changes. VO2max work supports those hard moments; sustained climbing and conservative pacing remain the spine.
3000 miles rewards fat oxidation. This volume work shifts your fuel mix so you're still burning fat at hour 5, not bonking at hour 3.
Race-pace efforts that mimic Race Across America (RAAM)'s demands. Pacing, fueling, and tactical decisions under fatigue. Practice the race before June.
At Race Across America (RAAM), changes in grade or pace can lift effort above threshold before it settles again. Over-unders train that transition while you keep riding.
175,000ft of climbing on grades that change every minute. You need to switch from seated to standing without losing rhythm.
58ft/mi signals a climbing-heavy course. Sustained sub-threshold and threshold work builds the steady power needed without turning the opening climb into the day’s hardest effort.

Road-specific control matters at Race Across America (RAAM). Practice on paved roads across the full diversity of American: use smooth gear and cadence changes, accelerate deliberately out of corners, and settle quickly back into sustainable power for 3000 miles.
Endurance with intensity spikes baked in. Exactly what 175,000ft of climbing on paved roads across the full diversity of American does to your power file on race day.
88–92% FTP is where you'll spend the hardest sustained miles of Race Across America (RAAM). Train it until it feels boring.
Low-cadence force work supports 175,000ft of climbing when the grade lowers cadence. Practice controlled torque while preserving good form.

race_overlay.heat: June in Oceanside, CA to Atlantic City, NJ — RAAM traverses every climate zone in the continental United States. Riders start in California coastal morning and within hours enter the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts where temperatures exceed 110F (43C). The Rockies bring freezing mountain passes above 10,000 feet. Kansas and the Great Plains deliver 95F+ heat, brutal headwinds, and violent thunderstorms. The Appalachians and Eastern Seaboard bring humidity, rain, and fog. All of this happens in a single continuous effort over 8-12 days with no shelter except what the crew provides. Begin heat acclimatization 10–14 days before Race Across America (RAAM) — 20–30min sauna sessions or midday rides in full kit. Pre-load sodium 48 hours out. Target 500–750ml/hr with electrolytes on race day. Race-day realities: Desert heat exceeding 110F (43C) through California, Arizona, and Utah; Eastern humidity and summer heat through the Appalachians.
race_overlay.nutrition: For a multi-day 3000-mile race, no single calorie total or one-food strategy is credible. Rehearse continuous intake while riding plus substantial meals at planned stops; document carbohydrate, fluid, and sodium intake, resupply cadence, and gut response. Use checkpoints and publicly available services only as the category rules allow, carry backup calories, and complete a full night-riding systems rehearsal.
race_overlay.altitude: Race Across America (RAAM) includes meaningful altitude exposure. Reduced oxygen availability can affect sustainable power, pacing, and recovery. Use a conservative upper-mountain pacing plan, test any travel or acclimatization strategy before the event, and plan layers for changing conditions. Do not begin iron or other supplements without clinician-guided testing.

pack_summary: This 10-workout pack focuses on Durability, Endurance, and VO2max to prepare you for 3000 miles of paved roads across the full diversity of american landscape in Oceanside, CA to Atlantic City, NJ.
